title: I rebuilt my game's whole UI and replaced 270+ character portraits with an AI-assisted pipeline. Here's the before/after and what actually worked
author: AlgondarAntillia
selftext:
I'm a solo dev making Antillia, an age-of-discovery exploration and trading game in Godot. Over the last few weeks I replaced almost every screen in the game and gave the recurring characters new portraits. AI tools were involved at most steps, so I wanted to share the workflow, including the parts that didn't work.



# 1. UI: rules first, then rebuild everything

The old UI grew one window per feature, so every screen had slightly different colours, fonts and buttons, and entering a building covered the whole town.

Instead of fixing screens one by one, I went in three steps:

1. **Mockups.** I generated mockups of the building screen, trading post, menus and sailing HUD to decide where information should live.
2. **Test screens.** I assembled the new layout in separate lab scenes fed with real game data, and checked long names, small resolutions and gamepad reachability there before touching the real game.
3. **Migration.** Town and buildings first, then menus and the sailing HUD, then events, naval combat and duels.

**What didn't work:** the mockups used a dark navy panel style, and on top of the actual town it looked pasted on. I kept the mockups' layout but switched the material to two-layer paper. AI mockups were great for deciding *where* things go and much less reliable for deciding *what it should feel like* in the actual scene.

The rules that came out of it:

* One paper panel style for panels, buttons and dialogs
* Colours defined in one place. Towns take on their culture's palette, while meaningful colours (buy/sell, ship roles) stay the same everywhere
* One currency icon and one tooltip style across the game

Because a coding agent did a lot of the migration, I leaned heavily on automated checks: headless probe scenes that verify layouts don't clip, that every control is reachable with a gamepad, and that old behaviour still holds. Without those, "it looks fine on the screen I checked" would have hidden a lot of breakage.

# 2. Portraits: from modular faces to dedicated art

The game has a lot of characters, so it uses a modular 2D portrait system (face shape, features, hair, outfit) that can make a face for anyone. The downside is that expressions and angles are basically fixed, and you can't refine one person's lines. For companions you spend hours with, that was a real limit, and playtesters said so too.

So recurring characters now get dedicated portraits. The pipeline:

1. Capture the character's existing modular portrait as a reference
2. Generate a line-art, cel-shaded portrait from that reference
3. Run a shared chroma-key and framing bake to a 1024 px transparent PNG
4. Register it, keeping the modular portrait as a fallback
5. Probes check framing, left/right facing, emotion icons and the fallback path

Right now that covers all 182 companions and every royal sponsor (93 unique artworks). Other NPCs still use the modular system.

**Two things I had to learn the hard way:**

* **Identity vs. "swapped parts".** One round changed the faces too much and the characters stopped looking like themselves. The next stayed so close to the modular preset that it still looked like assembled parts. What worked was treating the preset as a starting point: keep face shape, hair, eye and skin colour, but redraw the eyes, jawline, hair flow and how the hat, ears and collar connect.
* **Style drift.** If you use your newest output as the style reference for the next batch, the style slowly drifts toward semi-realism: smaller faces, bigger torsos, more rendering. I fixed it by always anchoring to the same two approved reference portraits instead of chaining.

# Disclosure

Generative AI tools were used during development for art, 3D models, music, sound effects, parts of the writing, and UI mockups, with my review and editing. The game doesn't generate anything with AI at runtime.

There's a free playtest on Steam if you want to see how it holds up in motion. I'm also happy to answer questions about the pipeline.

Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5117870/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5117870/)

comments.author: l0westL0wbob
comments.body: Why does it look like a snall color change and then a massive ai-fication on the portraits?

replies.author: AlgondarAntillia
replies.body: The portraits are exactly what they look like. A lot of playtest feedback said the old character art felt unpolished, so I rebuilt them using the old faces as references.

replies.author: l0westL0wbob
replies.body:
Maybe you could add more building variances, so it doesn't look like 50 times the same building with a different orientation.

Regarding the characters, maybe try to give them imperfections, let them age or get wrinkles, maybe some injuries, or dirt, or more face details like Glases, eye patches, jewelry etc

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body: I greatly prefer the "before" portraits. The brew ones just look so generic.

comments.author: kannazaki
comments.body:
Town , Shipyard , Fleet Menu , Character portraits looks much better and professional after.

Sailing HUD looks better before with light blue waves as if it's low ocean shipyard rather than deep shipyard , the dark blue ocean would look great if ur game is using a deep ocean shipyard.

replies.author: kannazaki
replies.body:
This is not a insult but the honest truth : The before portraits looks like as if we are treating cal-arts simplistic minimal character design as the Mona Lisa when it looks something like a kid drew it since there is some artistic talent behind it but looks unpolished.

This part is for the ppl saying the after char portrait are generic : *Dude the switch of artstyle for Teen Titans or thundercats to the bs cal-arts style in TTG / TG was so bad that they effectively ended that IP , even Ben 10 went cal-arts and lost everything* and those western shows has some amazing character design that was on par with anime of the era.

This is for who are gonna argue some Japanese anime do the same: *Yea a lot of Japanese anime do use that minimalistic char design but dude that is for a mini segment and has quality , even Panty & Stocking uses old school western char blocky models* but they make it look high quality since it's a deliberate design choice.

But here it's looks unprofessional if the developer is an artist and didn't bother to do an decent job and cut corners for it.

comments.body: Got to say that i like the before ones

comments.body:
Before ones had 'soul'. After ones have 'polish'.

I prefer soul over polish. But, everyone will have own taste I guess.

comments.author: Afraid-Molasses1103
comments.body:
I just don't understand why some people like this generic AI look the new portraits have. Why do you like them? They look like every other game that uses AI art, which makes it quite uninteresting, and the worst thing art can be, boring.

Some of the top row I like much better, some of it could be saved by some simple adjustments. Actually, the first character is decent. The rest could mostly have been fixed by correcting the eyes to make them more like the first, and removing or correcting the bridge of the nose, and adjusting the brow angles.

A shame to see stuff like this, when a little polish was all that was needed.

I just saw a comment that you are going to mix these 2 styles. Whatever you do, don't do that.
